title: CSRF protection for cookie based apps
when: A web app signs users in with cookies and has forms or fetch calls that change data, and cross site request forgery must be blocked.
inputs: how forms and fetch calls are built
prompt:
Goal: Every state changing request is shown to come from the app's own pages, through SameSite cookies, an Origin check and a token.
Steps:
1. GET, HEAD and OPTIONS never change data; every other method is checked.
2. First layer: the session cookie uses SameSite=Lax, or Strict for admin panels.
3. On POST, PUT, PATCH and DELETE the Origin header must equal the app origin from config; without Origin fall back to the Referer origin; with neither, refuse on browser routes.
4. Synchronizer token: 32 random bytes kept in the server session, rendered as <input type="hidden" name="csrf"> and sent from fetch as X-CSRF-Token; compare with timingSafeEqual.
5. Stateless choice: a __Host-csrf cookie plus a matching header, the token being an HMAC over the session id so a sibling subdomain cannot plant one.
6. Failures get 403 with code csrf_failed and a log line; issue a fresh token at login.
Quality bar:
- JSON only APIs still check Origin.
- Login and logout forms are protected too.
- A test with a foreign Origin expects 403.
Pitfalls:
- SameSite alone (old browsers, GET that changes state, sibling subdomains).
- Tokens in URLs, leaking through Referer and logs.
- CORS with credentials for any origin, which undoes every check.
Verify:
- [ ] All unsafe methods pass the check.
- [ ] A foreign Origin gets 403.
- [ ] Forms include the token.
- [ ] Tokens compare in constant time.
Output: csrf.mjs, form template updates, test/csrf.test.mjs.

examples.input: proteger os formularios do painel contra CSRF
examples.output: SameSite=Lax, Origin check on unsafe methods, session token in hidden field and header, 403 csrf_failed
